slide_title: Gas Exchange Surfaces: Human Lungs & Air Pathway
original_text: Gas Exchange Surfaces Human Lungs & Respiration Includes all structures that conduct air in a continuous pathway from the lungs Air moves from nose  pharynx  trachea  bronchi  lungs nFiltered, warmed, and humidified in this process nAt body temp and saturated with water once it reaches lungs Air passes from pharynx to glottis, followed by larynx (voice box)and trachea (windpipe) nLarynx and trachea permanently held open by cartilage rings nFacilitates air movement When food is swallowed nLarynx rises nGlottis closed by epiglottis nBackward movement of soft palate in mouth covers the entrance to the nasal passages
explanation: The human respiratory tract conducts air through a continuous pathway: nose, pharynx, trachea, bronchi, and lungs. During this passage, air is filtered, warmed, and humidified, reaching body temperature and water saturation before entering the lungs. The larynx (voice box) and trachea (windpipe) are held open by rigid cartilage rings to facilitate air movement. During swallowing: 1) the larynx rises, 2) the epiglottis covers the glottis (the opening to the larynx) to block food entry, and 3) the soft palate moves backward to cover the entrance to the nasal passages.

questions.q: What is the function of the cartilage rings in the larynx and trachea?
opts: To keep the airway permanently open for air movement
To absorb oxygen directly into the bloodstream
To secrete mucus to trap bacteria
questions.exp: Rigid cartilage rings support the larynx and trachea, preventing them from collapsing and ensuring a permanently open airway.

questions.q: What structure prevents food from entering the trachea during swallowing?
questions.exp: During swallowing, the larynx rises and the epiglottis covers the glottis, preventing food from entering the airway.
